newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai's private sector to remain minor player.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai's private sector to remain minor player.

text.p: Private businesses in Shanghai are growing fast in number, but they will always be a minor part of the city's economy, the secretary of Shanghai's Federation of Industry and Commerce said on Monday.
Shanghai may have been the launching pad of private enterprise in China, but the state will retain ownership of the lion's share of the city's economy forever, Zhang Yapei said.
"Private enterprise will always only play a supplementary role," Zhang said in an interview. "We can't have a system in which private companies play the primary role."

He predicted the growth of private businesses in Shanghai, much faster than the state-owned sector in recent years, would level off in the coming years with the state sector remaining strong and dominant.
Zhang said that in fact, China only needed private enterprise because it was underdeveloped.

"We need the market economy because China is backward. The state sector alone cannot serve every element of the economy, so there needs to be a supplement, and that supplement is the private and collective sectors," he said.
"But the private sector is only useful for handling the activities that the state sector cannot handle, for instance the service industries which make life easier for ordinary people," he said.
The number of private companies in Shanghai at the end of 1996 totalled 54,000, up from 39,000 the previous year, Zhang said. About 6,000 of them are members of the Federation.
Shanghai's private sector includes advertising firms, investment and stock consultancies, hi-tech companies and manufacturing as well as traditional services like restaurants.
But Zhang said both the state and the private sectors had limits beyond which they could go.

"We must educate and lead (private entrepreneurs) to understand that they play a supplementary role. People need to understand what their role is, and that you can't go beyond that role. If you're a horse, then you're a horse," he said.
The reform of China's bankrupt state-owned enteprises, when completed, will lead to a renaissance in the state sector of the economy, he said.

"The thing the private businesses are most scared of is the successful completion of the reform of the state enterprises," Zhang said. "The private enterprises know they can't compete with the state-run enterprises."

Zhang stressed that the Federation of Industry and Commerce was an organisation led by the Chinese Communist Party and only passed on to the government those views of its members which it considered to be reasonable.
"We do not represent the private companies, we lead and guide them," Zhang said.
He said the work of the federation included conducting educational work with private businessmen on the benefits of the socialist system and the leadership role of the Chinese Communist Party.
